pinterest.title: Samoan Wedding Traditions: Fine Mats, Orators, the Taualuga and the Family Feast
pinterest.description: Samoan wedding traditions are led by the aiga, the extended family, and its matai. The two families meet and their orators speak, the bride's family presents fine mats ('ie toga) to the groom's family, the church blesses the marriage, the bride dances the taualuga and everyone sits down to a shared feast. Our guide walks through each custom in the order the day unfolds, for Samoan-Australian couples marrying at home or in Samoa.

pinterest.title: 'Ie Toga: Why Fine Mats Are the Most Honoured Gift at a Samoan Wedding
pinterest.description: 'Ie toga are the highest-ranking item in the Samoan exchange system, and in Samoan marriage ceremonies the bride's family presents them to the groom's family. Each mat is hand woven with fibres so fine it can take months or years to finish, and some pass through several generations. In 2019 the fine mat was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Plan for heirloom mats with unhurried time and a dignified space.

pinterest.title: The Taualuga: The Dance That Crowns a Samoan Wedding Reception
pinterest.description: The siva is a slow, graceful storytelling dance, and the taualuga is the classical Samoan dance, "a dance of negotiation and celebration". At many Samoan weddings, the bride dances the taualuga to close the formal dancing while her family dances around her in support. Give it its own moment in the running order, with the floor cleared and the music agreed with the family. Our guide covers the dances, the dress and the rest of the day.

slides: Samoan wedding traditions you did not know, in the order the day unfolds
A Samoan wedding joins two families, not only two people. It is led by the aiga, the extended family, and its matai, in the way of fa'a Samoa.
The families meet: the tulafale, the orator, speaks for each side. The speeches honour the other family, acknowledge the guests and mark what is being given.
Fine mats ('ie toga) are the most honoured gift. In Samoan marriage ceremonies, the bride's family presents them to the groom's family. Some mats pass through generations.
The church service sits at the heart of the day for many Samoan families. The minister, and the family's faifeau if they have one, guides the order of service.
Many brides marry in a white gown for church, then change into a puletasi for the reception, often in fabric that matches the bridal party or the groom.
The taualuga is the high point. At many weddings the bride dances it to close the formal dancing, with family dancing around her. Then comes the feast, often from the umu.

instagram_carousel.caption:
A Samoan wedding is the meeting of two families, carried out in the way of fa'a Samoa.

Orators speak for each side. Fine mats change hands. The church blesses the marriage. The bride dances the taualuga, and the whole family sits down to eat.

There is no single script. Practice varies from family to family and village to village, and between Samoa and the communities in Australia, New Zealand and the United States. So the best first step is a simple one: ask both families what they expect.

Our guide walks through each custom in the order the day unfolds: fa'a Samoa and the matai, the families' formal meeting and speeches, the presentation of 'ie toga, the church wedding, the puletasi and lavalava, the siva and the taualuga, and the feast. It closes with what Australian couples need to know about marrying in Samoa, or bringing these customs into a wedding at home.
